title: Idiom or Nonsense?
intro: Some of these are real English idioms and some are invented. Decide which is which.

A2.why: Real: “a piece of cake” means very easy.
Invented: the real idiom is “a piece of cake”; for easy things with pie, we say “easy as pie”.
Real: “break the ice” means start a conversation when people feel shy.
Invented: you “break the ice” to start talking, never the glass.
Real: “under the weather” means a little ill.
Invented: a little ill is “under the weather”, not under the clouds.

A2.q: 'That car cost an arm and a leg.'
A2.why: Real: “cost an arm and a leg” means very expensive.

A2.q: 'That car cost a hand and a foot.'
A2.why: Invented: the real body parts are “an arm and a leg”.

A2.q: 'Can you keep an eye on my bag for a minute?'
A2.why: Real: “keep an eye on” something means watch it for a moment.

A2.q: 'Can you keep a nose on my bag for a minute?'
A2.why: Invented: you watch things with your eyes: “keep an eye on”, never a nose.

A2.q: 'Hold your horses! The stagecoach doesn't leave until noon.'
A2.why: Real: “Hold your horses!” means wait, don’t rush.

A2.q: 'Hold your cows! The stagecoach doesn't leave until noon.'
A2.why: Invented: the idiom is “Hold your horses!”, never cows.

B1.q: 'Don't spill the beans about the surprise party.'
B1.why: Real: “spill the beans” means tell a secret.

B1.q: 'Don't spill the peas about the surprise party.'
B1.why: Invented: secrets come out with beans: “spill the beans”.

B1.q: 'She let the cat out of the bag.'
B1.why: Real: “let the cat out of the bag” means reveal a secret by accident.

B1.q: 'She let the dog out of the bag.'
B1.why: Invented: it is always a cat in the bag, never a dog.

B1.q: 'We only meet once in a blue moon.'
B1.why: Real: “once in a blue moon” means very rarely.

B1.q: 'We only meet once in a red moon.'
B1.why: Invented: rare things happen “once in a blue moon”; the colour is fixed.
Real: “on the ball” means alert and quick to understand.
Invented: an alert person is “on the ball”, not on the wheel.

B1.q: 'Let's call it a day and finish tomorrow.'
B1.why: Real: “call it a day” means stop working for now.

B1.q: 'Let's call it an hour and finish tomorrow.'
B1.why: Invented: you “call it a day”; the idiom never changes to an hour.

B1.q: 'Don't count your chickens before they hatch: the job isn't yours yet.'
B1.why: Real: “don’t count your chickens before they hatch” means don’t celebrate too early.

B1.q: 'Don't count your eggs before they hatch: the job isn't yours yet.'
B1.why: Invented: the idiom counts chickens, not eggs, even though eggs are what hatch.

B2.q: 'You just have to bite the bullet and tell her.'
B2.why: Real: “bite the bullet” means do something unpleasant you have been avoiding.

B2.q: 'You just have to bite the sword and tell her.'
B2.why: Invented: the idiom is “bite the bullet” (perhaps from patients biting a bullet during surgery), never a sword.

B2.q: 'I've been burning the midnight oil all week.'
B2.why: Real: “burn the midnight oil” means work late into the night.

B2.q: 'I've been burning the midnight candle all week.'
B2.why: Invented: the lamp burns oil, so it’s “burn the midnight oil”; don’t mix it up with the real “burn the candle at both ends” (do too much, sleep too little).
Real: “jump on the bandwagon” means join something because it is popular.

B2.q: 'Everyone's jumping on the wagon wheel now.'
B2.why: Invented: people join a trend by jumping on the “bandwagon”, not a wagon wheel.

B2.q: 'The ball is in your court now.'
B2.why: Real: “the ball is in your court” means it is your turn to act.

B2.q: 'The ball is in your yard now.'
B2.why: Invented: from tennis, the ball is in your “court”, never your yard.

B2.q: 'Stop beating about the bush and just tell me.'
B2.why: Real: “beat about the bush” means avoid saying something directly.

B2.q: 'Stop beating about the tree and just tell me.'
B2.why: Invented: the British idiom is “beat about the bush”; no tree.

B2.q: 'After the operation, the doctor said I was as fit as a fiddle.'
B2.why: Real: “as fit as a fiddle” means very healthy.

B2.q: 'After the operation, the doctor said I was as fit as a violin.'
B2.why: Invented: healthy people are “as fit as a fiddle”; the instrument is fixed.

C1.why: Real: “cut corners” means do something cheaply or badly to save time or money.

C1.q: 'After the third defeat, he threw in the towel.'
C1.why: Real: “throw in the towel” means give up, from boxing.

C1.q: 'After the third defeat, he threw in the flag.'
C1.why: Invented: boxers give up by throwing in the “towel”, not a flag.

C1.q: 'You need to read between the lines here.'
C1.why: Real: “read between the lines” means understand what is hinted, not said.

C1.q: 'You need to read between the words here.'
C1.why: Invented: hidden meaning sits “between the lines”, not between the words.

C1.q: 'Losing that job was a blessing in disguise.'
C1.why: Real: “a blessing in disguise” is a problem that turns out well.

C1.q: 'Losing that job was a gift in disguise.'
C1.why: Invented: the fixed phrase is “a blessing in disguise”, not a gift.

C1.q: 'It's time you got your act together.'
C1.why: Real: “get your act together” means start behaving in an organised way.

C1.q: 'It's time you got your show together.'
C1.why: Invented: you “get your act together”, never your show.

C1.q: 'Don't scrap the whole plan; that's throwing the baby out with the bathwater.'
C1.why: Real: “throw the baby out with the bathwater” means lose the good part while removing the bad.

C1.q: 'Don't scrap the whole plan; that's throwing the baby out with the dishwater.'
C1.why: Invented: the baby goes out with the “bathwater”, never the dishwater.
